video_title: Lawfare Daily: FCC’s Bad Labs Rulemaking with FCC’s Andy Hendrickson and Alice Jou
transcript: [music] We're now implementing the covered list to look for foreign produced drones, routers, power inverters, and robotics. Our certification bodies are the first line of defense in checking whether a device that is submitted for authorization is on the covered list or is otherwise prohibited from receiving [music] an authorization. >> It's the LawFare podcast. I'm Justin Sherman, contributing editor at Lawfair and CEO of Global Cyber Strategies with Andy Hendrickson and Alice JW from the FCC's Office of Engineering and Technology. Our equipment authorization integrity [music] work streams, you know, ask who we can trust to evaluate the rest and those two pieces. I mean, they have to fit together. So if the gatekeeper is not accountable, [music] even a a very good rule at the gate becomes sort of harder to enforce. >> Today we're talking about testing labs and certification bodies for equipment sold in the US, how that apparatus moved offshore and the national security risks, and how the FCC is thinking about and proposing rulemaking on the problem. Let's start first with where you both work, which is the FCC's Office of Engineering and Technology. What does this office do? >> I think the easiest way to describe our office is that basically we make invisible infrastructure of modern life work. Every time your phone connects to Wi-Fi, your headphones pair over Bluetooth, uh an electric guitar works without cables, or your car communicates wirelessly, there's an enormous amount of engineering underneath that just seemingly is a simple experience. So our office actually helps write the technical rules that make all of that possible. We advise the rest of the FCC on engineering. We manage experimental licensing that so many people use to try out new ideas. We oversee the equipment authorization system, the process that helps ensure, you know, RF devices, radio frequency devices comply with FCC requirements before they enter the market. So the job isn't, you know, only about implementing policy to be honest. It's also, you know, about being able to find better ways to turn policy into systems that are useful, trustworthy, and accessible to people who rely on them. >> And as it relates to the covered list and why we're here, our office is the office that administers, as an Annie mentioned, the FCC's equipment authorization program. Um, and that's what gives the FCC the authority to regulate nearly every wireless consumer device imported and marketed in this country. This is how the FCC makes the covered list work through the equipment authorization program. And for your listeners, the covered list is a list of communications, equipment, and services deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to US national security or the safety and security of US persons. And this list is how the FCC can prohibit authorizations of new foreign produced drones, routers, robots, power inverters, everything you've been hearing about in the news today. >> There's actually an interesting historical example. In 1985, the FCC opened spectrum for unlicensed devices under certain technical conditions. Sounds a bit bureaucratic, but was actually a remarkable bet. you know, instead of the government deciding which technology should win, it actually established interference limits and let innovators kind of experiment. So that approach is really what helped make Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and an entire ecosystem that nobody could have designed in advance possible. I love the story because, you know, it's what's good engineering regulation can do, you know, create room for invention. And uh there's a second side to the story, too, right? So, a wireless device has to coexist with everything around it. You don't want your new gadget interfering with emergency communications or aviation, and you want its, you know, RF exposure to meet our limits. So, we have a relatively small team at the FCC lab in Colombia, Maryland that are actually overseeing the program that handles tens of thousands of applications annually. So, that I mean that only works because we rely on private testing laboratories, certification bodies, and accredititors. So the question becomes, how do we know we can trust the people at the gate? That's really the story we're here to discuss today. >> Well, that's a perfect segue. So, let's start by talking about that gate. And as many listeners know, and as you both alluded to, the FCC has been quite active lately. Uh I mean, in a number of regulatory areas with a national security nexus. uh some listeners may recall and if not you can go listen to our previous episode with Adam Chan to talk about some of that in the in the submarine cable space. In this case, as you mentioned, we're talking today about so-called bad labs. So, these refer to labs that review and approve electronics for use in the United States, but are ultimately owned or controlled by a foreign adversary nation. And so your rules, which we'll which we'll get into in more detail, are targeting these labs for a range of of potential national security reasons. So before we get to the the storming of the gates or or whatever the the metaphor is there, let's start with a grounding in one, how do US devices get approved? And then two, what are the FCC's authorities with respect to that process? >> Hm. Okay. Well, I think of it as three layers really of assurance. First, the test lab puts a device through its paces. You know, engineers measure where it transmits, how much energy it emits, whether it stays within the applicable limits, uh whether it might interfere with other services. It's actually very physical work. There's shielded rooms, calibrated instruments, antennas, cables, repeatable measurements. And then second, you know, there's a telecommunications certification body, what we call a TCB, which reviews the technical record against our rules. It can ask questions, you know, request additional information and where appropriate require more testing. So for devices that require certification, that body issues the authorization. And then third, an accreditation body assesses whether that testing lab and certification body are competent to actually perform those functions. So the FCC establishes the requirements and recognizes the organizations participating in the system kind of a clever way at a scale like we don't need a government engineer personally testing every wireless product but it rests on a basic premise. Those independent organizations must be technically competent, candid about their work and accountable when something goes wrong. So a lab report isn't just a PDF, you know, it's evidence on which a public regulatory decision depends. So, and that means integrity is not an optional extra. So, Alice can certainly explain the legal authority better than I can, but from an engineering standpoint, this is very straightforward. A system is only as reliable as its measurements and verification process. >> Yeah. So, I can step in on the legal authority. We've been saying this a number of times throughout the year. The FCC has an quiet superpower. Uh section 302 of the Communications Act gives the FCC this broad durable statutory authority to regulate consistent with the public interest the interference potential of any device that is capable of radiating radio frequency energy. Um that can be anything with an antenna. So your Bluetooth, your Wi-Fi devices. It also includes electronics that radiate RF energy. So your VoIP telephone, your surveillance camera, if it's plugged in via Ethernet or some other way, it can still cause static in your devices, in your other devices. And we we regulate that as well. That whole regulatory scheme for devices has existed for 60 years. Think about all the things that Andy was mentioning, the invisible infrastructure, but think about all the products and devices you use and you trust. Your drugs have to be tested. Your products are tested for safety. Our labs are part of this whole system where labs that are deemed competent can trust for these different regulatory frameworks. About 30 years ago, Congress amended our section 302 authority to give us explicit authority to set standards for private test labs and certification bodies. We're not just looking at the technical skill of the lab under our statutory authority. We're looking at the qualifications and the standards. What we're now doing is we're insisting on better oversight, accountability, and reciprocity when we evaluate these very important gatekeepers to our system. And the role of these TCBS, the certification bodies is actually more important now in this new role that the FCC is playing on national security. Since last December, the FCC has been administering the covered list, which now names entire categories of communications equipment by country of production. Right? So, we're now implementing the covered list to look for foreign produced drones, routers, power inverters, and robotics. Our certification bodies are the first line of defense in checking whether a device that is submitted for authorization is on the covered list or is otherwise prohibited from receiving an authorization. So the integrity of these certification bodies, these test labs matters a lot. >> So when did testing move offshore outside the boundaries of the US? Or maybe that's not even the right way to phrase it. Was it always offshore and it's become more offshore or how do you characterize that that shift? >> Well, I think the short answer is that it gradually was moving offshore then all at once it happened, right? So, our equipment authorization data tell a striking story. In 2007, the United States accounted for about 31% of applications by testing firm location. And by 2025, it was below 4%. So over that same time period, the share associated testing firms in China rose from about 15% to roughly 82%. So that's extraordinary change in less than two decades. So then naturally you ask, well, why did that happen? Well, manufacturing moved, of course, and companies naturally like to test close to where they build products, but policy incentives mattered, too. So, historically, reciprocal treatment was an important part of the international acceptance. We recognize your testing capability and you recognize ours. Over time, FCC placed greater emphasis on accreditation and technical competence even when the foreign market didn't provide comparable access to American labs. So, in other words, access became a one-way street in some places. So, I want to pretend that one regulatory change explains every decision a manufacturer may have made. Labor costs, you know, manufacturing clusters, supply chain efficiency, all of that matters as well. But if you design a system in which testing anywhere can serve the US market while US firms cannot necessarily compete on equal terms abroad, shouldn't be surprised when the capacity shifts, right? So that that if if you take a look at the chart, it's worth looking at because it it makes the lesson visible. Um we didn't wake up one morning and decide to concentrate on our testing pipeline in just one country. thousands of rational individual decisions uh were made under the rules uh we created produced you know sort of a strategic dependency is what I would call it. So that's the kind of thing a regulator has to be willing you know to see and correct. Yeah, I mean as you said some of so many of these supply chain shifts particularly in technology are are are structural in so far as to your point there's there's so many uh economic factors and a variety of other uh corporate decisions and so forth that that end up shifting the bounds. You mentioned the one-way street and I like that phrasing and so to latch on to that next. The US is not the only country, as you're saying, that requires certification, but as you noted, there are many other countries that that do not allow foreign bodies to make those determinations. So, just for examples, what are some of those quote unquote non-rescrocal countries? And why is that a meaningful data point? Perhaps if you're looking at where some of the bodies making certifications for our products are geographically located. >> I think we can name China, Switzerland, India as some examples of countries who don't have reciprocal trade agreements, reciprocal economies with us. We are looking at the way that we've set up our system to allow testing from anywhere in the world. even if those countries don't accept our test results from our test labs. That is one way that our industry has gotten gutted over the last 20 years. >> Okay. Yeah. I I mean I can imagine as you're saying I mean you don't I mean you can respond to this or you don't don't have to respond to this, but I can imagine as you're saying there's sort of two tracks which are at least perhaps in some ways intersecting, right? They're sort of the economic piece of of countries like the PRC that obviously for years have imposed a wide variety of barriers on foreign firms specifically to to shut down market access and competitiveness and so forth. And so there's an economic dimension, but then I'm also envisioning a national security dimension where there are indeed other countries, perhaps the PRC included, that would see the prospect of having a country like the US or someone else certify equipment used over there and have no interest in in doing it from a national security perspective. So So back to the United States, because as we're saying, there's so much to get into with your rule making. give us more insight into the process maybe even just historically of how these test labs and certification bodies get approved. How much information historically have they had to provide to the US government as part of those approvals and and who owns that approval process? I >> can just give you a big picture view of the test labs and the certification bodies that we have in our system. Currently, we've got about 600 test labs, about 40 certification bodies that the FCC is recognized and approved for to test and certify within our system. So, if you're if you're a device manufacturer, you want to come to market, you look for a test lab that is recognized by the FCC. These test labs under our rules are required to have a technical accreditation. It's called the ISO7025. It's a general competence standard, international standard that checks the competence of your lab, that you calibrate your equipment, that you have processes in place to make sure you're supervising your tests, that you're keeping your records. That kind of stuff happens. And when the FCC recognizes a test lab, that test lab is recognized for two years at a time. This gives the accredititor time to assess the test lab's competence against this international standard. They look at the test lab procedures and competence every two years. It's traditionally been seen as a historically a technical competence standard. But this international standard also includes standards for how you can trust the test lab results are good. And and one of the things we are looking at these days is whether you can trust this test lab because of where it's located. In the past, nobody asked who owned this test lab, what laws applied to the employees who are running the tests. That matters because our rules require test results when they're submitted as part of an equipment authorization application to be signed under penalty of perjury by the person who conducted or supervised those tests. So you can imagine what can happen if the people who are signing these test results, who are vouching for them, are coming from a test lab where maybe the penalty of perjury doesn't scare them as much because US law may not apply over there or maybe hard to enforce. >> Yeah. So I think I think if we step through it, it's the ISO, you know, 17025 accreditation. FCC gets a chance to review recognize it specifically with OAT within OAT. So acceptance as an FCC recognized test lab happens. There's a reacreditation uh and FCC review every two years with the ongoing eligibility contingent on this technical competence and compliance with FCC integrity and national security requirements. And I would also just add that from an ongoing compliance perspective that we retain FCC retains authority to withdraw or decline recognition if a lab demonstrates any type of deficiencies, loses accreditation, fails to meet these FCC requirements, or otherwise no longer satisfies applicable criteria for competency, independence, reliability, trustworthiness, or you know, some of these national security requirements we're talking about. Recently the FCC in this vein has been looking at some specific foreign labs for national security reasons. So talk to us about the recent certification body in Minnesota and I'm putting air quotes around Minnesota and what the FCC has publicized that it did and if you want to add on you know what authorities were used there and is that something that the FCC has done historically or is this a a newer focus for the commission? >> Justin, thanks for raising this issue. We think it's very important. Recently we discovered a certification body by the name of Derrycom that wasn't being truthful about where it was located. Uh and this is because in our system we have test labs and we have certification bodies. And while the test labs have largely migrated overseas, the certification bodies are still required under our laws to be located either in the United States or in a reciprocal economy. We found a TCB dairycom that was registered in our system under a Minnesota address. But what we found was that all of its testing was actually happening overseas in a non-rescrocal economy. Derrycom actually only was approved for our system in October 2024. And within 18 months, it came out of nowhere from being a brand new certification body in our system to being the number four certification body out of 40 total certification bodies. So in less than 18 months, it had certified almost 12,000 applications by volume. It was really growing very quickly. We spoke with some of our regulator counterparts in Canada. This DairyCom certification body was the number two body up in their market. We looked into this because we had never heard of this company before. We Googled the address that Daircom gave us in Minnesota. When you look up our filings, you can look it up. The pictures we saw of this building was a tiny building. Based on some of our experienced engineers, a building that size could not have held the kinds of equipment, the anooic testing chambers, the spectrum analyzers, everything of the staff that you would need to be able to certify 12,000 applications like that. We started an investigation. We started asking some questions. Uh the reality of what we found was that the owner of this certification body is a Chinese citizen. He owned 99% of Daircom. Five of the six employees, the managing director, the quality manager, the administrative staff, they all were based in Shenzen or in China. There are four other contract technical reviewers also in China. It turns out Derrycom never did any work in Minnesota beyond showing up in person for the accredititation assessments that they needed to pass in order to be approved into our system. And the only way we found out about this was that we opened an investigation. We sent letters to that Minnesota address and we heard back from a US person located there. He was the person who signed a declaration who swore under oath that DerryCom, these employees never worked at the site. They never staffed the site. His company never tested for DairyCom. He never performed any technical work for Derrycom even though in our records he was listed as being its technical reviewer. And the point of this was that this person, this US person was subject to US laws. Um he could be compelled to explain what happened. But the other folks who were part of Derrycom who filed all this false information about where Derrycom was doing the work, they're all outside of US law. They sit in Shenzhen. That's why it's so important that we can enforce our laws, that our certification bodies and our test labs are located in jurisdictions that allow the FCC to oversee uh and enforce and ensure accountability for these critical gatekeepers in our system. So once we found out that Derrycom wasn't telling the truth in its filings, we spoke with the accredititor. The accredititor then suspended Dairy Comm. So they've no longer been in our system since May of this year. And just last month, the FCC issued a citation to DairyCom. The legal authority about that was related to um the false statements that Dairy Comm made about where it was located. And that's always been a violation of FCC rules, not telling the truth to your regulator. There are some other technical violations as well related to dairycom. When these certification bodies get accredited and approved for our system, there are certain scopes where they can do certification and do reviews. This company Derrycom claimed to be testing certain types of devices at certain frequency bands that were just outside of their accredititation. They weren't supposed to be certifying these types of devices and they did. The takeaway there is really just don't lie to the FCC. Don't try to lie to the FCC or game the rules to get into the system. We do have very experienced, competent staff who will be able to review these certification bodies, these test labs. We are looking at the statements you make with the FCC and we're able to ensure the integrity of our system. I think this is important for for two reasons as a case study. I mean, one, as we're saying, this is certainly alarming. Although, if we look at any number of, you know, BIS documents, justice.gov indictments, etc., etc., etc., uh sort of fits within uh a number of known, you know, potential activity areas that that foreign nation states undertake with setting up uh I mean whether this was or not, you know, setting up fronts elsewhere and and trying to slip under the radar. The second is I think as you're saying this important broader policy statement that this revelation makes which is that as Andy noted earlier we've had for a variety of reasons offshoring of these testing and certification processes much like we've had offshoring of a variety of other technology areas from the US in the last you know 20 odd years but in this case yet again there's this sort of acute security risk that until recently it seems has not gotten proper scrutiny. So pivoting then to what that scrutiny looks like, this so-called bad labs rule, can you summarize the new FCC rules around Bad Labs? And then within those rules, what is if any major points of continuity from from what was happening previously and what are the major points of change? We informally call it bad labs, but when you look at how our proceeding has unfolded and and the formal title of this proceeding is the equipment authorization integrity proceeding. Really, we want to increase the integrity and strengthen the trust that you have in our system. Our very first action was about bad labs. We were trying to keep untrustworthy actors out of our system. Last spring in April, we were trying to reward trusted labs. We were giving some of trusted labs a fast track into our system, getting quicker device approvals if they tested in the US or reciprocal economy. So what we have teed up for a vote later this month at the end of October is really about trust and reciprocity that in order to be part of the US device testing system you need to be located in a reciprocal economy and reciprocity is the price of entry into the US device market. So what we are proposing to do is that the FCC would stop recognizing test labs, certification bodies, and accredititation bodies based in non-rescrocal economies. I >> I think of it sort of as a three-part effort, not three disconnected rules, right? So first, you know, we addressed who should not be allowed to control the gatekeepers. So that's the commission's 2025 action restricting participation by labs, certification bodies and accreditation bodies, you know, owned or controlled by prohibited entities. So that's about, you know, keeping clearly identified national security risks out of the system. And then as Alice mentioned, you know, in April 2026, we the commission adopted, you know, measures to reward trusted testing and improved oversight. So there's a positive incentive there. For certain technologies, requiring a pre-approval guidance, testing through a trusted lab can support, you know, a more streamlined path itself. We also want better information about the people and locations that are actually doing the work and stronger surveillance after you know products reach the market. So and third one you know she Alice just mentioned as well is now before the commission you know the question is about whether we should stop recognizing testing from non-rescrocal jurisdictions after some sort of transition period you know rather than trying to police the structural problem one lab at a time so I mean we haven't voted on this yet so that you know that next step so just want to be precise we're talking about a proposed policy you know and the case for it so simply I mean I would put The covered list helps determine which equipment cannot be authorized. Our equipment authorization integrity work streams, you know, ask who we can trust to evaluate the rest. And those two pieces, they mean they have to fit together. So if the gatekeeper is not accountable, even a very good rule at the gate becomes sort of harder to enforce. >> And one thing we should add for your listeners, there's a very clear transition date. We're proposing to stop recognizing test labs in non-rescrocal economies on December 1st, 2028. We want to give the economy, the industry time to transition away from untrusted labs or labs in untrusted or non-rescrocal economies. And that date is December 2028. In addition to that factor, are there other tradeoffs that are are top of mind for you across you just mentioned in part an economic one, but any other economic factors, national security, etc. as you think about the the changes and subsequent enforcement of potential changes? >> Well, I think there are real trade-offs and I I don't think we should, you know, wave them away. you know, a company may have a testing relationship that works for it today. You know, moving to another lab can involve cost, you know, scheduling, capacity, engineering, just coordination in general. So, those are real operational concerns, especially for smaller manufacturers. But testing is typically a product development and compliance expense. You know, it's not a cost that repeats for every individual unit that they're selling. you know, the cheapest test isn't always the lowest cost outcome. So, if a flawed report triggers, you know, a retest or delays a product launch, the savings evaporate pretty quickly. We should, you know, be comparing the full cost of a reliable authorization process, not just two prices, you know, on a lab quote. So, capacity, you know, is really the harder question, I think. Can reciprocal economies absorb the demand? um how fast can labs add chambers, instruments, train people? That's why I think the transition period really matters. You don't rebuild an ecosystem by flipping a switch. Uh you establish, you know, clear destination, give industry a credible runway to invest in. And our job is to is to take the implementation concerns seriously without losing sight of what we're trying to protect, which ultimately the integrity of the process, the resilience of the supply chain itself. Right? So a system that is cheap in normal times but fragile when stressed can turn out to be very expensive indeed. >> Just to editorialize for a minute as I like to point out right once once a number of things get into a supply chain it is a lot harder uh usually to get them out after the fact. So certainly well taken and that's a good point as well about about the need to consider the aggregate costs of a particular process rather than as you as you put it the sort of quotes on on a piece of paper or a marketing sheet. So just to zoom in on this a little bit further before we zoom back out is obviously one challenge we've seen in many other conversations about de-risisking and decoupling US tech supply chains from China is that they can run into structural and logistical constraints that sometimes the more ambitious security focused goals cannot grapple with. So for example, you know, I think of parts of the supply chain where it would take too long to onshore things relative to whatever a time horizon might be or types of technologies where where severing that crossber connectivity entirely is just not feasible in the current world. So, I'm just curious at a I guess deeper and higher level here at once. Is it the goal to, you know, one day we'll have all device testing and certification within the United States? If so, is that realistic and on what time? And if not, you know, what's a more reasonable and secure balance? Again, as you said, noting the potential significance of the national uh security threats at play. >> Sure. Well, I think it's an important correction to the premise, right? I the goal is not to move every single test lab to America. I mean, we certainly want more American capacity. I mean, absolutely. But we also want, you know, a geographically diverse network of reciprocal partners that can handle the workload. That's the difference between, you know, onshoring everything and reducing sort of a dangerous concentration. The engineering side is manageable, though it isn't effortless. I mean a lab needs shielded space as I mentioned calibrated instruments, procedures, accreditation, you know, and people is probably the one of the most important things who understand how to do and interpret the measurements. So some specialized capabilities, you know, take longer to build than others. It's probably the biggest constraint in my view is human capital. You can purchase a spectrum analyzer faster than you can develop an engineer, right? who who knows what the output means or when it's wrong. I should probably say we should give industry a predictable, you know, transition and let companies make investment across the US and partner economies. You know, some work will move to existing facilities with available capacity, some will require an expansion, some will require training new technicians, and we should listen carefully to evidence about bottlenecks rather than just assuming every category of testing is interchangeable. Right? So I you know what gives me confidence is that you know this is a solvable systems problem. We know what a competent lab looks like. We know how to measure capacity. We know how to accredit. The challenge is really to align the incentives and execute not to invent an entirely new industry from scratch. >> Without getting into obviously anything you can't divulge, where do you see the FCC's thinking about this risk space headed next? >> Three words I think. um you know verify uh watch modernize you know what I mean by that is you know verify that the organizations doing the work are who they say they are uh operating where they say they operate you know with the personnel and capabilities they claim to have. So watch the system you know after an authorization because a grant should not be the end of accountability and you know modernize is really the data tools so suspicious patterns stand out sooner. I mean, here's an example of what I mean. So, if if two unrelated products come in with suspiciously identical measurements, a modern system should help flag that for an engineer to examine. You know, not necessarily at human scale. There should be automation doing this type of work. So, software won't replace technical judgment, but it can make the judgment much more effective. So, we shouldn't depend solely on someone happening to notice a strange table in a PDF or two documents that share the same size. So the same is true I think for broader national security responsibilities as equipment restrictions become more sophisticated. The people reviewing applications need better information, clearer guidance, trustworthy partners, and we also need to work with other parts of government because supply chains and trade arrangements don't stop at the FCC's organizational chart. Right? So I see a chance to make a legacy program genuinely modern, more datadriven, more transparent to responsible participants and quite honestly better at detecting problems before they propagate through thousands of devices. >> Policy makers and others these days of course are debating certification regimes for a host of other national security relevant technologies these days. obviously AI applications um being one, but hardware and uh various others. So, I'm just curious uh if you if either of you and and would love to hear from both of you on this. Are there any lessons in general from for others thinking about tech certification regimes, national security that you think Bad Labs and the work you're doing here might offer for, you know, principles, practices, whatever that might be for for other uh areas. >> I think there's a couple big lessons we've learned, especially in OT. I mean first foremost data data matters right so the FCC's equipment authorization system contains just an extraordinary amount of information about our technology supply chains but data you know is only valuable if you have the chance to look at it and when we have and when we did we we uncovered how quickly US device testing you know had moved overseas and become concentrated in a single non reciprocal economy creating a significant dependency for the country implement presentation really matters. So I think that's number two. Writing rules is important, but rules only have value if they're sort of followed and enforced, right? So a key part of our work is making sure that the system functions as intended, supporting those who follow the rules and ensuring accountability for those who do not. And the third thing I would mention is, you know, capability. It matters. So the decline of the US test lab industry was mirrored by, you know, the FCC lab itself in the sense that it's why we're reinvesting, you know, and rebuilding in it with new leadership, with modern equipment, new generation of engineers. More broadly, we want to help rebuild America's device testing workforce and technical expertise. >> All of these tech certification regimes, they're going to be collecting incredibly valuable data. Uh but that data doesn't mean anything if it's not being interpreted and judged by people. And one of in addition to all the new generation of engineers that we're bringing into the lab oet we're also investing in new attorneys. Um and this year we're bringing in an entirely new cohort of attorneys. Actually this week we onboarded a new cohort of attorneys. Um and they come from organizations your listeners will be familiar with. They come from the private sector, from the big law firms, from the justice department. We have folks from the commerce department, BIS, office of ICTS, startups as well. Um, we're also investing in our existing FCC attorneys. We're bringing on folks laterally who have deep telecom and rulem and policy experience. Uh, we're investing in this because it matters. We can't just collect the data, collect the licenses. We need skilled attorneys to look at the data, to look at what we're collecting and make sense of it and then act on it. That's what we're doing. We're look, we're going to be doing more investigations into these labs. We think we're going to find more as we look more closely at our data and as we get leads, as we're working with our engineers in the lab. >> That's all the time we have. Andy Alice, thanks very much for joining us. >> Justin, thank you. >> Thank you. The LawFare podcast is produced by the LawFare Institute. Check out our written work at lawfare media.org. The podcast is edited by Jen Patia and our audio engineer this episode was Cara Schillan of goat rodeo. [music] Our theme song is from Alibi Music. As always, thank you for listening.
